Equity, diversity, and inclusion are fundamental values of the American Library Association and are one of ALA’s committed key action areas which act as guiding principles for investment of energies and resources.
ALA’s Office for Diversity, Literacy and Outreach Services also encourages using a social-justice framework of diverse perspectives within LIS to advocate for equitable access to library services for all people.
In an increasingly diversifying country, library and information professionals are in need of critical thinking skills, cultural competency approaches, and new social justice approaches to executing equitable information spaces.
Currently, LIS programs, professional organizations, and LIS-based companies are competitively offering trainings around Information Equity, Diverse Communities, and Critical Librarianship approaches to LIS.
For example, the New England Library Association (NELA) held a one-day diversity summit in the summer of 2017 with full enrollment, heavily focused on discussing race, racism, gender, sexuality, ability, immigrant and migrant rights, and social justice applications to diverse groups.

The University of North Carolina’s School of Information and Library Science offers a Diversity Advocate Certificate, the LIS press “Library Juice Press Academy” offers a course titled “Exploring and Applying Critical Theory: An Introduction for Librarians,”, and Library Journal has a number of diversity based professional development workshops such as “Diversity and Cultural Competency Training: Collections & RA,” to name a few.
This graduate track is a highly manageable 12-credit program from an accredited institution of higher education.
The proposed track in Information Equity, Diverse Communities, and Critical Librarianship approaches will prepare LIS graduates for diverse workplaces, serving and collaborating with diverse populations, and recruiting a more diverse workforce, as well as creating equitable information institutes.
This proposed track will be the only such track in New England and as a track, it will also serve librarians across the United States.

Information Equity, Diverse Communities, and Critical Librarianship supports URI’s mission by supporting diverse communities.

CCJ 285 and CCJ 456 have been approved by the CCJ faculty as criminal justice elective options for majors and CCJ 334 has been approved as a criminology elective. CCJ 285 (Fac Sen Bill # 23-24-19) and 456 (Fac Sen Bill # 24-25-01) have been fully routed and approved through the curriculum process. CCJ 334 is currently being routed through the process (submitted for the October 14 A&S curriculum committee meeting) but we seek to include the class in this NOC of change to reduce the need for curriculum modifications moving forward as the department intends to offer this class as soon as the 25-26 AY. BFA Theatre, Effective Fall 2025 Appendix B Changes approved for addition of THE200 to the curriculum per Faculty Senate Bill # 22-23-39A passed and signed by President on 23.04.20. This course (THE200) replaces two previous courses: THE291 (2 cr) and THE391 (2 cr). It is intended to make the production courses less complicated and confusing for students, allowing for consistency of the numbering system.

COLLEGE OF EDUCATION: BS Health & Physical Education, Effective Fall 2025 Appendix C Curricular changes are intended to align with national norms and availability of university course offerings.
The changes will offer students flexibility to select professional electives that closely align with their unique career goals in health and physical education.
COLLEGE OF THE ENVIRONMENT & LIFE SCIENCES: BS Geology & Geological Oceanography, Effective Fall 2025 Appendix D The current program has two options (Geology option and Geological Oceanography option).
We propose to add the Water and Climate Sciences as a third option.
The total number of credits in intro & professional courses, core geosciences and option specific courses, electives and supporting sciences is not changing, i.e. the number of credits will be comparable to the currently existing options.
However, option specific core course GEO 200, GEO 234 and GE0 280 replace GEO 210, GEO 320, GEO 370 and GEO 450.
Please refer to the advising sheet for the new Water and Climate Sciences option.
Copies of the existing (unchanged) advising sheet for the other two options are included for reference.

No new courses need to be created for the proposed changes.
Existing courses added to the revised core program are taught at a frequency that ensures degree completion in four years.
All existing classes have the capacity to accommodate additional inflow of students or, if needed, new class sections can be opened.
Students in the current options will not be affected by the proposed changes.
NEW SPECIALIZATIONS COLLEGE OF THE ENVIRONMENT & LIFE SCIENCES: Specialization in Water & Climate Science (BS Geology & Geological Oceanography), Effective Fall 2025 Appendix E The specialization in Water and Climate Sciences allows students the flexibility to define their own area of concentration within the water and climate sciences.
Example areas of concentration include environmental geology/ hydrogeology, and climate.
Students will be well prepared to pursue careers in environmental consulting, water resource management, sustainability initiatives, climate adaptation and resilience, and the emerging field of climate analytics.
These career opportunities are available with national and international government agencies, non-profit organizations, and the private sector.

The program will also equip students for research roles both in academia and the private sector.
Specialization Requirements: - All of the following courses: GEO200, GEO234G, GEO280, GEO305G, GEO483; GEO420 and/or GEO422; GEO482 and/or GEO484 - 24 credits of GEO courses at the 300-level or above

COLLEGE OF HEALTH SCIENCES: Specialization in Kinesiology (BS Kinesiology), Effective Fall 2025 Appendix F The Kinesiology Track provides flexibility to choose professional electives appropriate for a wide range of health and exercise science related careers. It is appropriate for students interested in pursuing health care professions such as physical therapy, chiropractic, medical doctor, or physician’s assistant or in becoming an exercise physiologist, strength and conditioning specialist, occupational therapist or health coach. Career opportunities exist in corporate, community, commercial and hospital-based fitness and wellness centers. The Kinesiology track will also prepare students for graduate study in clinical exercise physiology, cardiac rehabilitation, exercise science, health fitness, health promotion, preventive medicine and related fields. Kinesiology students will be prepared to become a certified professional in specialty areas including exercise physiology, strength and conditioning and/or personal training. One of: PSY 200, STA 220, 307, or 308 2. 12 credits from the list of professional electives, with a minimum of 6 credits from KIN courses: CHM 105, 124, 126; CMB 210; EDC/HLT 401; KIN 125, 243, 369, 375G, 414, 425, 464G, 482; NUT 360; PSY 255. Other KIN or health-related courses may apply with approval from the KIN Department Chair. Additionally, there are free electives.
